body:
**Retail trader base rates**
- SEBI FY22-FY24 study (Sept 2024): 93% of ~1.13 crore individual F&O traders lost money over FY22-24; aggregate losses > ₹1.8 lakh crore. — [News On Air (Govt.)](https://www.newsonair.gov.in/sebi-study-reveals-individual-traders-face-severe-losses-in-equity-fo-segment) [F]; [Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/markets/capital-market-news/sebi-study-exposes-massive-losses-for-individual-f-o-traders-in-india-124092400948_1.html) [F]
- SEBI FY22 study (Jan 2023): 89% (9 in 10) of individual F&O traders lost money in FY22. — [Business Standard, Jan 2023](https://www.business-standard.com/article/finance/9-out-of-10-individual-traders-in-f-o-segment-making-losses-123012600435_1.html) [F]
- SEBI FY25 study (July 2025): 91% of individual F&O traders lost money; net losses rose 41% to ₹1,05,603 crore from ₹74,812 crore in FY24. — [Business Standard, July 2025](https://www.business-standard.com/markets/news/net-losses-of-traders-in-fo-widens-in-fy25-sebi-study-125070701221_1.html) [F]
- SEBI FY25-FY26 study ("Profitability of Individual Traders in the Equity Derivatives Segment (FY25-FY26)", Aug 2026): 87.7% of individual traders lost money in FY26 (vs 90.9% in FY25); 82.1% lost even before costs; aggregate losses ₹91,685 crore in FY26 (FY25 revised to ~₹1,11,788 crore); average loss per trader ~₹1.17 lakh; active traders fell ~18% to 87.5 lakh (one outlet says 78.6 lakh — conflict); options ~92% of losses, futures loss rate ~66%; 43% of traders under 30; transaction costs ~₹25,000 crore in FY26 (brokerage ~44%, STT ~27%). — [SEBI on X](https://x.com/SEBI_updates/status/2090451964626894921) [F]; [Finnovate summary](https://www.finnovate.in/learn/blog/sebi-fno-trader-losses-fy26-individual-derivatives) [F]; [Coinswitch](https://coinswitch.co/switch/personal-finance/sebi-profitability-report/) [F]; [Open Magazine](https://openthemagazine.com/business/sebi-fo-loss-study-explained-why-9-in-10-retail-traders-lost-91685-crore-in-fy26) [F]. (Figures via secondary sources; SEBI PDF not opened.)
- Brazil (Chague, De-Losso & Giovannetti, 2019/2020): of individuals who began day trading mini-Ibovespa futures in 2013-2015 and persisted ≥300 days, 97% lost money, only 0.4% earned more than a bank teller's wage (top individual ~US$310/day), and no evidence of learning. — [RePEc/IDEAS](https://ideas.repec.org/p/fgv/eesptd/525.html) [F]; [Quantpedia summary](https://quantpedia.com/retail-day-trading-is-an-uphill-battle/) [F]
- Taiwan (Barber, Lee, Liu & Odean 2014): using complete TSE data 1992-2006, less than 1% of day traders are able to predictably earn positive abnormal returns net of fees; past top performers do continue to earn ~38 bps/day while the rest lose. — [JFM 18:1-24 (IDEAS)](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/finmar/v18y2014icp1-24.html) [F]; [Working paper PDF](https://faculty.haas.berkeley.edu/odean/papers/day%20traders/Day%20Trading%20Skill%20110523.pdf) [F]
- Barber & Odean (2000): US households that traded most earned 11.4% annually vs 17.9% for the market (1991-96) — overtrading destroys returns. — [JF, DOI 10.1111/0022-1082.00226](https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00226) [K]

body:
`insight:marks-on-the-couch-2016` | confidence: verified | date: 2016-01-14

Memo of 14 Jan 2016 (written amid the China/oil sell-off). Core line: 'in the real world, things generally fluctuate between "pretty good" and "not so hot." But in the world of investing, perception often swings from "flawless" to "hopeless." The pendulum careens from one extreme to the other, spending almost no time at "the happy medium"'. Investors' failings take 'two primary forms: selective perception and skewed interpretation' - noting only positives (or only negatives), and reading the same event bullishly or bearishly depending on mood; 'rarely are their perceptions and interpretations balanced and neutral.' He also flags repeated failure to see 'ramifications and second-order consequences' (e.g., underestimating contagion from sub-prime 2007-08). Actionable: when Indian market narratives go to extremes (e.g., 'India can only go up' in 2024 small-cap froth; 'India is uninvestable' in 2013 taper or Mar-2020), write down the base-case reality ('pretty good'/'not so hot') and compare to what prices imply.

Sources:
- https://www.oaktreecapital.com/docs/default-source/memos/on-the-couch.pdf

body:
1. **At an Indian cost of equity of 12–13%, the DCF calls almost every quality compounder 60–70% overvalued.**
   - The terminal value on these settings is worth ~11–15x NOPAT (`(1 − tg/ROIC)/(r − tg)` = 0.8/0.075 ≈ 10.7x at 25% ROIC), while these stocks trade at 48–52x.
   - So for Indian high-P/E names the **"IRR the price offers"** line (7–8% here, against a 12.5% hurdle) and the reverse-DCF growth line are the useful outputs, not "value −65%".
   - The decision gate uses the 5-year multiple against the index hurdle, not DCF value against price, so the strict CoE alone does not decide the card.
2. **The exit multiple is the hidden bet.** Every Indian scenario's exit P/E (25–50) was 2–3x its DCF-consistent P/E (12–17). The worksheet now prints both and flags the gap. A 5-year multiple that needs the market to keep paying 40x is a bet on market behaviour, and the card should say so.
3. **The base-rate class can be badly biased.** Our only 5-year Indian class (random NSE survivors from Sep-2020, x3 = 44%) started six months after a crash low and ran through a small/mid-cap bull market. Every model probability looked "0.05–0.14x the base rate", and the card flags that departure. Part of the gap is the class's bias, part is the starting P/E (≥35x; `insight:india-mb-starting-pe`). We need a delisting-inclusive, multi-start-date class from stage 1 (see §4).
4. **The soft-flag gate binds first.** All three practice deep dives ended with 6–8 open flags and no variant view. That is consistent with what the deep dives themselves said ("no position without a variant view"). The card makes the rule mechanical.
5. **Unknown hard rules are common.** H3 (rating non-cooperation) was never checked in any practice run, and H5 stayed unresolved at VMM. The protocol needs an explicit stage-2 checklist step before the card (add it to protocol v1.3).
6. **Missing inputs show up.** None of the practice files had an own 10-year P/E history, ADV or a usable FIVE price. A deep dive must now collect: 10 FY-end P/Es, 3+ peer P/Es, 6-month ADV, and a dated close.

body:
- Screener's "Borrowings" includes lease liabilities, so asset-light retailers look indebted.
- Goodwill from a PE buyout crushes reported ROE and ROCE. Use return on tangible equity.
- Ind AS 116 EBITDA overstates margins of rent-heavy models by 4–6 pp. Always find the pre-Ind AS number (company presentation, or EBITDA − lease cash outflow).
- Viral social-media "ground data" can be fake (the VMM guard-recruitment meme was disowned by the company).
- Payback and SSSG are company-defined. Read the definition before quoting them.
- (v1.1) **Cost-plus transfer pricing caps margins.** Exports sold to the parent at cost + x% do not gain from a weak rupee. The parent captures it.
- (v1.1) **High ROCE can be borrowed from the group's balance sheet.** If the constrained product is made by a sister company, the listed entity's capital looks small.
- (v1.1) **Cost allocations from the parent can step up without notice** (Cummins: support services ₹111 → ₹223 cr in a year, then a further Q2 "true-up"). Read the other-expenses note every year, and the call's "one-offs" answer every quarter.
- (v1.1) **Company "ranges" can hide the number.** "DC = 30–40% of power gen" is ±₹130 cr a quarter, wide enough to hide a slowdown in the rest of the business.
- (v1.2) **US GAAP gross margin is not comparable across retailers.** Some put occupancy, distribution and buying in COGS (FIVE); others put them in SG&A. Compare operating margin, or rebuild merchandise margin.
- (v1.2) **One-off credits inside COGS.** FIVE's Q2 FY26 GAAP gross margin of 48.5% included a $163.6M tariff refund. Trailing GAAP EPS screens are wrong for four quarters. Always read the Ex-99.1 reconciliation.
- (v1.2) **Ownership-filing false alarms.** Vanguard's 13G/A shows 0% after its Jan-2026 realignment. The 13F still shows the shares.
- (v1.2) **"Average sales per store" usually counts only stores open the full year.** Also compute total sales ÷ average store count.
- (v1.2) **FCF in a slowdown-of-openings year is flattered** (capex and working-capital timing). Normalise before using it.
- (v1.2) **Tool notes:** use `sec_fetch.py doc T ACC --file NAME --text` for exhibits; `holdings13f` value can misparse (use shares); confirm the insider "non-10b5-1" flag on the form.
- (v1.1) **Tool note:** `tools/nse_fetch.py transcripts SYMBOL --download DIR` ignores `--from/--to` and downloads everything. List first, then fetch only the URLs you need.
- (v1.3) **"Decadal-low GNPA" can be write-off driven.** Rebuild the NPA walk: at Federal Bank Q2 FY27 write-offs (₹498 cr) exceeded fresh slippage (₹420 cr).
- (v1.3) **Special funding windows inflate both sides.** FCNR-backed loans turned +4% core retail growth into +18% headline.
- (v1.3) **PCR can be bought with a windfall.** A one-time tax-refund gain funded a buffer provision; PCR 76.6% → 87%.
- (v1.3) **Undiluted P/B and ROE flatter a bank with warrants outstanding.** Put the dilution in the denominator first.
- (v1.3) **Conservative guidance makes a credibility score look excellent.** Measure guidance bias, and compare with peers.
- (v1.3) **Rating-agency and company KPI definitions differ** (credit cost 67 bp vs 41 bp; "top-20 group" vs "top-20 borrowers"). Copy the definition with the number.
- (v1.3) **Tool notes:** `nse_fetch.py results` is stale after Dec-2024 (use `integrated`); bank websites may be behind a bot wall (Pillar 3, some transcripts) — fetch by hand and pass `--local`; pdftotext scrambles multi-series deck charts (prefer XBRL and press releases).
